runs.text:
A **context window** is the amount of information an AI model can use at once when generating a response. Think of it as a workspace holding the instructions, conversation, and reference material available for the current reply. The model uses that information to decide what to say next.

Its size is measured in **tokens**, which are small units of text: a word, part of a word, or a punctuation mark. For English text, one token averages roughly four characters, though this varies. A model with a 100,000-token context window can handle a large amount of text, but some of that capacity may need to be reserved for its answer, depending on the model’s limits.

When you send a message, the application assembles the input for the model. This may include system instructions, previous messages, your latest request, and material retrieved from files or tools. The model processes that context and generates its reply one token at a time, using the available input and the tokens it has already produced.

If a conversation grows too long, not everything can fit. The application may remove older messages, summarize them, or select only relevant portions to include. That is why an assistant can appear to “forget” something from earlier: the original detail may no longer be available in its current context. Even when information fits, the model is not guaranteed to notice or use every detail correctly.

A context window is different from both **training knowledge** and **persistent memory**. Training shapes the model’s general capabilities; the context supplies information for the current response; and a separate memory feature, if present, can save information for later use. For reliable results, keep important instructions clear, provide relevant source material, and restate crucial details when a conversation becomes long.

messages.content: What are the most common pests?

Slugs and snails are the usual culprits in damp climates, along with aphids, caterpillars and the odd rabbit. Check leaves, including the undersides, every few days so you catch trouble early. Picking pests off by hand, using copper tape round pots, and covering brassicas with fine netting all work without chemicals. Encourage ladybirds, hoverflies and birds, which eat many pests for you. A tidy garden helps, because slugs shelter under old leaves and planks.
What is crop rotation?

Crop rotation means growing different families of vegetables in a different part of the garden each year. Pests and diseases that target one family build up in the soil if you plant it in the same place, and each family takes different nutrients. A simple plan uses three groups: roots such as carrots and beetroot, legumes and onions, and brassicas such as cabbage and kale. Move each group along one bed every year and the cycle repeats every three years.
Can I grow vegetables in containers?

Yes, and many do well. Use pots with drainage holes and a good multipurpose compost, and give each plant enough room: a tomato wants a pot at least thirty centimetres across, while lettuces and herbs are happy in a window box. Containers need more frequent watering and feeding than beds, because nutrients wash out. Put them where they get plenty of light, and group them together so they shelter each other from the wind.
When is the last frost, and why does it matter?

The last frost is the final night of spring when the temperature drops below freezing, and it varies with where you live. Tender plants such as tomatoes, courgettes and beans are killed or badly damaged by it, so they should only go outside after it has passed. Ask a neighbour or check local records to find your average date. Hardy crops like peas, broad beans and onions can be planted earlier. A sheet of fleece will protect young plants on a cold night.
How do I know when to harvest?

Each crop gives its own signs. Courgettes are best small, at about fifteen centimetres, and keep producing if you pick them often. Tomatoes should be fully coloured and slightly soft. Lettuce can be picked leaf by leaf from the outside, which lets the plant keep growing. Carrots and beetroot show their shoulders above the soil when they are ready. Harvest in the morning when plants are cool and full of water, and pick regularly, since leaving fruit on the plant slows new growth.
What does mulching do?

Mulch is a layer of material spread over the soil, such as compost, bark, straw or grass clippings. It keeps moisture in, stops many weeds from sprouting, protects roots from temperature swings and slowly feeds the soil as it rots. Apply it about five centimetres deep in spring, once the soil has warmed and been watered, and keep it clear of plant stems so they do not rot. Top it up every year as it breaks down.
Which tools do I actually need?

You can manage with very few. A spade and a fork for digging and turning compost, a hand trowel for planting, a rake for levelling the soil, a pair of secateurs and a watering can with a fine rose are enough for a first year. Buy the best you can afford, because cheap tools bend and break. Clean them after use and keep them dry, and a sharp edge on your spade makes digging far easier. Borrow anything else, such as a wheelbarrow, until you know you need it.
How do I deal with weeds?

Pull weeds when they are small, before they flower and drop seed, and the job stays manageable. A hoe slid just under the surface on a dry day cuts off young weeds quickly. Perennial weeds with deep roots, such as dock and bindweed, need digging out with as much root as you can lift, because any piece left behind will regrow. Mulch and close planting both shade the soil and reduce weeds. Little and often beats one big clear-out.
Are herbs easy to grow?

Many are among the easiest plants there are. Mint, chives, parsley and thyme thrive in pots and forgive missed waterings. Mint spreads aggressively, so always keep it in its own container. Basil likes warmth and sun and does best indoors or in a sheltered spot. Pick often, since regular cutting keeps herbs bushy and stops them flowering too soon. A few pots by the kitchen door mean you will actually use them when you cook.
Are raised beds worth the trouble?

For most beginners, yes. Raised beds warm up sooner in spring, drain better in wet weather, and let you fill them with good soil whatever lies underneath. Because you never walk on the soil it stays loose and easy to work. A bed about a metre and a quarter wide lets you reach the middle from either side. Timber, sleepers or even old scaffold boards will do for the sides. They cost more to set up, so start with one and see how you get on.
How should I plan the year?

Work backwards from the seasons. In late winter, decide what you want to eat and order seeds. In spring, sow hardy crops first and tender ones after the last frost. In summer, water, feed, weed and harvest steadily, and sow a few quick crops like radishes every fortnight so there is always something ready. In autumn, clear beds, add compost and plant garlic and broad beans. Write down what worked so next year starts from experience.
What should I feed my plants?

Rich soil does most of the work, so start by adding compost or well-rotted manure before planting. Hungry crops such as tomatoes, squashes and potatoes benefit from a liquid feed every week or two once they flower or fruit. Leafy crops like spinach and kale appreciate extra nitrogen early on. Follow the instructions on the pack, because too much feed gives soft, leafy growth that pests love and can burn roots. Container plants need feeding more often than plants in the ground.
Can I grow fruit in a small garden?

Yes. Strawberries thrive in pots and hanging baskets, and a single fruit bush such as a blackcurrant or gooseberry will crop for many years in a corner. Apples and pears can be trained flat against a fence as cordons or espaliers, which uses very little space. Raspberries are easy but spread, so give them their own bed. Choose self-fertile varieties if you only have room for one tree, and water fruit well while it is swelling.
What about growing potatoes?

Potatoes are a rewarding first crop and grow well in large bags or a deep bed. Buy certified seed potatoes and let them sprout on a bright windowsill for a few weeks, which is called chitting. Plant them about fifteen centimetres deep in spring, and draw soil up around the shoots as they grow so the tubers stay covered and do not turn green. Early varieties are ready in about ten weeks; maincrops take longer but store better.
Can I save my own seed?

You can, and beans, peas and lettuce are the easiest to begin with. Let a few of the healthiest plants go to seed instead of eating them, and wait until the pods or heads are dry and brown before collecting. Spread the seed out to dry fully indoors, then store it in labelled paper envelopes somewhere cool and dark. Seed saved from hybrid varieties, marked F1 on the packet, will not come true, so use open-pollinated types instead.
Do I have to thin out seedlings?

Yes, and it feels ruthless but it works. Seedlings that are too close compete for light, water and nutrients, so none of them grow well. Thin in stages, removing the weakest first, until the plants are at the spacing shown on the seed packet. Snip them with scissors rather than pulling, so you do not disturb the roots of the ones you keep. Thin carrots in the evening, because the smell of bruised leaves attracts carrot fly.
How can I attract pollinators?

Plant flowers alongside your vegetables. Open, simple blooms such as marigolds, borage, calendula and cosmos are loved by bees and hoverflies, and they bring beneficial insects that eat aphids too. Let a few herbs flower, and avoid spraying insecticides, which harm the good insects as well as the bad. A shallow dish of water with stones for perching helps in hot weather, and a small pile of logs gives solitary bees somewhere to nest.
What should I do in winter?

Winter is a quieter season, but not idle. Clear spent plants, spread compost or manure over the beds and leave worms to draw it down. Clean and oil your tools, wash pots to remove disease, and check stored produce for rot. Hardy crops such as kale, leeks and winter lettuce can keep cropping under a cloche or fleece. Use the time to plan next year, order seeds and mend fences and raised beds before spring arrives.
How much time does a small garden take?

A small plot needs about two to three hours a week in the busy months, spread across a few short visits. Spring is the heaviest, with sowing, planting and preparing beds. Summer is mostly watering, weeding and picking. Autumn and winter ask for very little. Watering by hand can be the biggest chore, so mulching, a water butt and sensible plant spacing all save time. Little and often suits most people better than a long session once a week.
What is the single most useful tip for a complete beginner? Two sentences at most.
